deep.reconstruction:
The page is spherical trigonometry on a sphere with centre O. It has two independent pieces, and both are standard.

(I) In- and excircle radii of a spherical triangle ABC.
Set a+b+c = 2s. Let rho be the inradius and rho_b the radius of the excircle opposite B, the one touching side b. The first figure shows the triangle with both circles. The excircle's tangent lengths are measured along the extensions of the sides.
Riemann writes four relations:
(1) sin(s-a) = cot(A/2) tan(rho). Equivalently tan rho = sin(s-a) tan(A/2). This is the right triangle formed by vertex A, the incentre and the tangency point on side c (or b). The tangent length from A is s-a, and the angle at A is A/2.
(2) sin s = cot(B/2) tan(rho_b). Equivalently tan rho_b = sin s tan(B/2). The tangent length from B to the excircle opposite B is s, and the excentre lies on the internal bisector of B.
(3) sin(s-c) = tan(A/2) tan(rho_b). The tangent length from A is s-c. The excentre lies on the external bisector at A, so the relevant angle is (pi-A)/2 and tan rho_b = sin(s-c) cot(A/2).
(4) sin(s-a) = tan(C/2) tan(rho_b). This is the analogue of (3) at C, with tangent length s-a.
These are the exact spherical analogues of the plane formulas r = (s-a) tan(A/2), r_b = s tan(B/2) = (s-c) cot(A/2) = (s-a) cot(C/2).
[My addition: with tan^2(A/2) = sin(s-b)sin(s-c)/(sin s sin(s-a)) they combine to
- tan^2 rho = sin(s-a)sin(s-b)sin(s-c)/sin s, and
- tan^2 rho_b = sin s sin(s-a) sin(s-c)/sin(s-b).]

(II) The volume of the tetrahedron OABC and the 'sine' of the trihedral angle at O.
The vertices A, B, C lie on the rays from O. The sides a, b, c are the angles BOC, COA, AOB. Let beta be the spherical altitude (arc) from B onto side b, as in the small figures.
- Area of face OCA = (1/2)·OC·OA·sin b.
- The height of B above the plane OCA is OB·sin beta.
- So the volume is P = (1/3)·area·height = OB·OC·OA·sin b·sin beta/6.
- Hence 6P/(OB·OC·OA) = sin b sin beta.
The altitude cuts the triangle into two right spherical triangles. The rule 'sine of a leg = sine of hypotenuse × sine of the opposite angle' gives sin beta = sin a sin C = sin c sin A.
Therefore sin b sin c sin A = sin a sin c sin B = sin a sin b sin C. This is the same symmetric quantity, 6P/(OA·OB·OC), whichever altitude is used.
Dividing gives sin A/sin a = sin B/sin b = sin C/sin c. This is the spherical law of sines; Riemann starts writing 'sin A/sin a ~'.
In short, this is the volume proof of the sine rule. Along the way it identifies the invariant sin b sin c sin A, the 'sine of the solid angle' at O.

Context: the previous page is about invariants of binary forms. The next page is a letter draft with upside-down sketches of triangles and circles, apparently continuing this kind of elementary geometry. The page looks like routine working or teaching notes, probably from around 1850.
errors: No mathematical errors found; all four radius relations and the volume and altitude relations are correct.
Minor notational looseness only. The volume denominator, transcribed as 'B', is surely 6, as the later line 6P/(OB·OC·OA) confirms. Several capital C's should be lowercase c (sides).

'P = OB·OC·OA·sin b/B·sin beta': the denominator is 6, not B.
'sin beta = sin C sin A' should be 'sin beta = sin c sin A' (lowercase side c).
'sin b sin C sin A' should be 'sin b sin c sin A'.
The last term on that line is 'sin a sin b sin C', not 'sin c sin b sin a'.
